title: Three gaps and a missed crossing

data.source: The three-gap theorem (Steinhaus; Sos, Swierczkowski, Suranyi 1958) and Sturmian words (Morse and Hedlund 1940). Numerical check on four irrational rotations, 40 more random ones, and noisy copies, seeded.

prediction: With the crossing interpolated the cuts sit at two points and the waits take two neighbouring values in balanced order (T1); restarting from the sample that crossed gives a constant wait and at most three gap lengths (T2); a monotone sampled occasion then has surplus twice the overshoot, not zero (T3); and noise of one part in a million destroys the three gaps (T4).
baseline: The three-gap theorem and Sturmian words; a null of random points through the same gap counter; and a decoy rule, "as many gap lengths as points".
why: All four statements held. Three of them are the three-gap theorem and the theory of balanced words, which are true of any rotation whether or not anyone mentions CRR. The fourth is arithmetic, and it carries a caution: in sampled records a perfectly monotone occasion shows a surplus of twice the overshoot, so reading R3's "surplus zero" straight off samples fails.

alternatives.null_worlds: 40 random steps: at most three gaps on 40, two balanced waits on 40. 300 random points: 300 gap lengths.

operating_characteristics: Identity room: theorems about rotations and one line of arithmetic. No outcome weighs for or against CRR as a claim about the world.
second_check: Adapted and re-run by a worker who did not write the mapping. No person has reviewed it.
variants: V-mathematical-3 (discrete time; the whole room is this museum experiment, not the owner's CRR)
